title: SONEL electricity sale to AES
point: Douala, Cameroon's main city and seat of AES-SONEL (approximate)

lenders.name: World Bank
lenders.role: The third Structural Adjustment Credit (SAC III, 1998–2004, US$180 million) listed completing privatization of public utilities as a key goal. Pineau (2004) calls the sale a commitment to meet one of SAC III's requirements.

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: Cameroon's December 2001 letter of intent reported to the IMF that SONEL's privatization had been completed, alongside pending sales of the water company SNEC and telecoms firm CAMTEL.

conditions: World Bank SAC III: complete the privatization program, especially public utilities (Pineau 2004). IMF letter of intent, 28 December 2001, reports SONEL privatization as done.

companies.name: AES Corporation
companies.role: Sole bidder; bought 56% of SONEL in July 2001; contract never published

companies.name: Actis
companies.role: Bought AES's 56% stake for US$220 million in 2013–14; company renamed ENEO

community: The concession set tariff rises above inflation of 5% (2001) and 7.5% a year (2002–2004). The low-voltage 'social' block was cut from 110 kWh a month to 50 kWh in 2004. Medium-voltage fixed charges jumped from 9.125 FCFA per kW a year to 2,500–4,000 FCFA per kW a month. The aluminium smelter ALUCAM kept paying 5 FCFA/kWh. Blackouts became much more frequent; a French Development Agency estimate cited by Pineau puts the growth loss at about 1%. A lawyer reported at least 57 court cases seeking compensation for outage losses. About 360 workers took early retirement.
outcome: Load shedding continued into the 2020s (Journal du Cameroun, cited on Wikipedia). A December 2011 law provided for transmission to be placed under public management; the state firm SONATREL was created in 2015 and began operating in April 2018 (Wikipedia).

title: IMF wage limits and health workers before Ebola
point: Freetown, Sierra Leone (approximate; the study covers Sierra Leone, Guinea and Liberia)

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: Ran programmes in Guinea for 21 years, Sierra Leone 19 and Liberia 7 between 1990 and 2014 (Kentikelenis et al. 2015).

conditions: Kentikelenis et al. The IMF says its programmes in all three countries had no wage bill limits from 2000 to 2014.

title: Jordan 2018 income tax protests
point: Fourth Circle near the Prime Ministry in Amman, where nightly protests gathered (approximate)

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: Signed a $700 million, 36-month Extended Fund Facility with Jordan in 2016. Passing the income tax law was needed before the programme's second review could go ahead (Jordan Times).

The final law (late 2018) set thresholds at JD20,000 for families and JD10,000 for individuals (Jordan Times).

outcome: Thirty-three unions struck on 30 May. Prime Minister Hani Mulki resigned on 4 June; his successor Omar al-Razzaz withdrew the draft on 7 June (MERIP). A revised law passed in late 2018 and took effect in 2019 (Jordan Times).

point: Lusaka (approximate; rural schools were hit hardest)

title: Malawi 2023 kwacha devaluation
point: Lilongwe, seat of the Reserve Bank of Malawi (approximate)

title: Greece 2012 Minimum Wage Cut and Athens Riots
point: Syntagma Square, in front of the Greek parliament

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: Co-lender in Greece's second bailout of about €130 billion from the EU and IMF (NBC/AP); party to 'Memorandum 2' (Eurofound).

lenders.name: European Commission and ECB
lenders.role: The other two troika members that set the Memorandum terms (Eurofound).

conditions: IMF Country Report 12/57 (March 2012), Greek letter of intent: 'an immediate realignment of the minimum wage level ... by 22 percent', a freeze to the end of the program, and a further 10% cut for under-25s, as a prior action. Also: collective agreements limited to 3 years, after-effects of expired agreements cut to basic pay and four allowances, and an end to arbitration requested by one side only. Act 4046/12 of 14 February 2012 adopted the loan agreement and Memorandum with the troika (IMF, EU, ECB). Under it, a cabinet decision of 29 February 2012 let employers cut minimum wages by 22%, and by 32% for workers under 25, without worker consent; contracts in the broader public sector that ran until retirement became open-ended contracts that could be ended under standard rules (Eurofound). NBC/AP: the bill was needed to unlock about €130 billion and also cut about one in five civil service jobs.
community: The basic gross minimum wage for a single worker fell from €751.39 to €586.08 a month; net pay fell to €476.35, or €426.64 for under-25s (Eurofound). About 100,000 people protested in Athens on 12 February 2012; unrest spread to six other cities (NBC/AP).
suppression: Police used tear gas and stun grenades. About 50 officers and at least 55 protesters were hospitalised; 45 people were arrested and 40 detained. Rioters set at least 45 buildings on fire (NBC/AP).
killed_note: No deaths reported in the sources.
outcome: Parliament approved the bill with 199 of 300 votes; 43 governing-party MPs who voted against were expelled from their parties (NBC/AP). The GSEE union asked Greece's Council of State to cancel the wage decision and sought ILO support (Eurofound).

title: Ireland Water Charges

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: Co-lender in Ireland's €85 billion EU–IMF bailout of November 2010 (Irish Times).

lenders.name: European Commission and ECB
lenders.role: Co-signers of the Memorandum of Understanding (Oireachtas answer, 2013).

conditions: The November 2010 Memorandum of Understanding set a timetable: 'water charges will be introduced in 2012 or 2013', with meters installed first, and water moved from local councils to a new utility (Irish Times, 2014). A 2013 parliamentary answer stated that the Memorandum with the EU, IMF and ECB 'provide for the introduction of domestic water charges'.
community: Charges began on 1 October 2014; a typical family of two adults and two children faced about €278 a year (Fox/AP; Irish Times). Tens of thousands refused to pay (AP); only 43% of customers paid in the first billing period (Irish Times timeline). Residents in Cork and Dublin blocked meter installation from 2014. About 100,000 people joined water protests in October 2014 (Irish Times timeline), and organisers said at least 100,000 marched on 1 November 2014 (AP).
suppression: After a protest at Jobstown, Tallaght, on 15 November 2014, where prosecutors alleged Tánaiste Joan Burton was kept in her car for up to three hours, eight people were prosecuted for false imprisonment. A 17-year-old was convicted in the Children's Court; charges against one man were dropped; six men, including TD Paul Murphy, were unanimously acquitted in June 2017 (RTÉ).
outcome: Charges were suspended in 2016 and billing was formally abolished in April 2017 (Dáil vote 96 to 48). Refunds followed; about 180,000 cheques were processed in the first week of November 2017 (Irish Times timeline).

title: Mexico 1982–1987 IMF Program Subsidy and Wage Cuts

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: Three-year Extended Arrangement of SDR 3.41 billion ($3.75 billion) approved 23 December 1982 after a November Letter of Intent (IMF history); CSM reported $3.9 billion in IMF credits. Disbursements were suspended in September 1985 (countrystudies).

title: DR Congo 2002 Mining Code
point: Kolwezi, heart of the Katanga copper and cobalt belt (approximate)

lenders.name: World Bank
lenders.role: The code 'was based on a draft prepared under the auspices of the World Bank' (Radley, The Conversation). IPIS notes the code was drafted by the DRC with the Bank.

conditions: A new mining code drafted with World Bank help to reopen industrial mining to foreign investors after the 1996-2003 wars (Radley; IPIS). Terms: 30% profit tax, 2% royalty on copper and cobalt, and a 5% state share in new projects (Radley).

outcome: Revisions first sent to parliament in March 2015, then suspended, were being revisited around 2017; the draft would raise copper and cobalt royalties from 2% to 3.5%, profit tax to 35% and the state share to 10% (Radley).
